utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody in and around the courtroom. Could you please call the case, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-81-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Perisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Could we have appearances for the day starting with the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Dan Saxon, Bronagh McKenna, and Carmela Javier for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much Mr. Saxon. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom. Mr. Perisic will be defended today by Mr. Novak Lukic and Mr. Boris Zorko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Gajic. Just to remind you that you're still bound by the declaration you made at the beginning of your testimony to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Gajic, good afternoon once again.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We shall continue where we stopped yesterday. You might remember that at the end of the day of yesterday we spoke about some of your colleagues who originated from the territories where the war was waged. You mentioned some names. You mentioned your colleague from the security administration, Mr. Svilar. You told us when he retired. Do you know whether since -- whether between 2003 and the day of his retirement he was promoted?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, yes, he was, from the rank of lieutenant-colonel to the rank of colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will continue with this subject. So the relationships between the three armies, and could we please focus on the security-related issues, because this is exactly why you are here as a witness. Yesterday, you told us -- this is on page 79 of our working transcript. I asked you about the contacts, and you told us that these were ad hoc contacts. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As the institution, the security administration, did you request from the security organs of the Army of Krajina and security organs of the Army of Republika Srpska to send any reports to you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, we didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you request from them to provide specific information on some specific events or incidents to provide some specific facts?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, they were entirely independent in making any decisions as to what they would report to us in our security administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Still, you didn't answer my question. Do you remember whether on any occasion you requested from them to provide any specific information?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether you requested from the security organs of the Serbian Army of Krajina and the security organs of the Army of Republika Srpska to come to any meetings at the security administration?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have yet another question which is related to the general tasks and responsibilities of the security administration that we discussed yesterday, but we did not raise this issue yesterday. Was the security administration tactically responsible for certain materials, equipment of the Army of Yugoslavia? Was there any specific document regulating that responsibility?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the security administration was tactically responsible for equipping units of military police with special equipment, and it was also tactically responsible for equipping security organs with material and technical equipment, as we called it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you give us any example for the sake of Their Honours, so possibly if you could illustrate what kind of equipment we are talking about that the security administration was responsible for.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, if we are talking about the equipment of the military police, we can talk about protective vests, for example, some special weapons. So automatic weapons also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I just interrupt.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Handcuffs as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I see the interpreter is struggling to keep pace. Can you just slow down a little bit, both of you, and give each other some time after speaking to allow the interpreter to interpret. Thank you. Carry on, Mr. Gajic. What else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. So this was related to the equipment of the military police. If we are talking about the equipment for the security organs, then these were different devices for intercepting telephone conversations or surveillance, also devices for searching apartments and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I may just ask. At page 3 -- I beg your pardon. Yes. At page 4, line 3, you also mentioned automatic weapons. What kind of automatic weapons are these? What are these weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we are talking about handguns, pistols, or rifles which had snipers or silencers, and they were used for any -- any conflicts with terrorists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic, do you know whether the security administration as a body that was technically responsible sent any -- or received, rather, any requests from these two armies for the equipment, the weapons of the kind that you just described, and whether the security administration responded to such requests?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, as far as I remember, there was only one request which came from the Serbian Army of Krajina for a certain quantity of such special equipment, and they provided a list of desired equipment. It came to us through the General Staff, and we were asked to respond. As far as I remember, there was also a note of the Chief of the General Staff who said, if we can, to provide some of this equipment but without endangering the situation of our military police, and we answered that we did not have any equipment that we could provide them with because we did not even have sufficient equipment for our own units. We only had some smoke boxes that we could provide to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who was responsible in the security administration to respond on behalf of the security administration as to whether you can provide them with the desired equipment or not?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was the chief of the security administration, and when we are talking about the military police units, he responded following a proposal that he received from the chief of the military police department.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yesterday when I asked about the names in the security bodies of these two armies, you mentioned some of the names. So now I have a few questions related to the security officers from the Army of Republika Srpska. You mentioned three names, Tolimir, Salapura, and Beara. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: During the war did you see any of those three individuals and where?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I saw all of them occasionally when they came to Belgrade. They would visit their families, because the families of all three of them lived in Belgrade. So on those occasions they would also come to the security administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So to make it more precise, you saw them on the premises of the security administration.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When they came to the security administration, were their visits pre-arranged? Were they announced? Did you know they would come?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, in case of General Tolimir, as a rule he never announced his visit. Captain Beara occasionally announced that he would come, and Colonel Salapura, given that he was chief of the military intelligence administration, as far as I remember, he only came once to my office.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You know which period we are interested in, so after you came back to the security administration in 1994. So when you say "occasionally," what do you mean more specifically? Was it once in a month, once in a week, or three times a week? So in the period between 1994 and the end of December 1995 when the war ended.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, when I said "occasionally," this means that they would come once every three to five months.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When they came to you, for example, Mr. Beara, did you ask any information from him? Did you request any information in writing or oral reports? So what was that discussion all about that you had with him?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, when Mr. Beara, who was chief of the security administration of the Army of Republika Srpska, when he came, he would provide us with an oral description or his estimate of the security situation in Republika Srpska, and he would generally speak about combat operations, and what we were particularly interested in were any implications that this could have for the security of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and our army, because this was our fundamental task as I explained yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you give us an example? So in the entire territory where the war was waged, what was it that you were interested in? What was it that could have had any implications for the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, these were combat operations that took place closer to our border. So it was possible for certain armed groups to cross the border whether illegally or in any other way and thus come to the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Furthermore, we were interested in learning about paramilitary units that were present in that territory because these also involved citizens of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and this is what we were interested in, to learn about them if they had such information, because such citizens were armed, and therefore they also represented a threat for the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. And obviously we were also interested in smuggling, particularly smuggling of arms and military equipment. Just -- let me just provide you with one example. At that time, a single bullet for a Kalashnikov rifle was worth $3.00 on the black market, and obviously tens of millions of such bullets of different calibres were smuggled.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did the security administration of the Army of Yugoslavia have any of its people, so to say, or their informers in the Army of Republika Srpska and the Army of Serbian Krajina? So regardless of the official security organs.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, no, we did not, because we thought that the information we received from the official organs were sufficient for us. And we also had some operational sources of our own which we inherited from the former JNA, and they were situated in the territory of Croatia or Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did the security administration have the right to set up its own operation centres or forward the posts in third countries, outposts in third countries?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't the security administration; it was the military intelligence administration of the General Staff of the VJ that had the right to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please explain for the benefit of the Chamber what the powers are of the intelligence administration in relation to third countries?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the intelligence administration can set up outposts in third countries abroad based on assessments or perceived needs. It can set up one or more intelligence centres. Such an intelligence centre would normally have several people working there with a back-up unit. There would be chiefs there and a number of operatives and logisticians. This is not a public installation. Rather, it is a covert one. They use operative communication lines, agents, and intelligence technology in order to gather such intelligence as I explained yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about the army of whichever country the intelligence centre happens to be based in, are they normally aware of any exchange of information going on in that way?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Normally that is not the case. These are normally covert operations, and the country normally doesn't know. The building itself may be camouflaged or disguised in some way. It may, for example, bear the name of a -- of a nonexistent company, whereas in fact it is an intelligence centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We know that you were educated in Germany as well. Setting up of intelligence centres such as this, is that something that is an established practice in other armies across the world?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic, that is definitely the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What does it mean to process a person in operative sense? What is the operative processing of a person?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, operative processing is normally undertaken in relation to persons already suspected of engaging in some sort of activity, but it must be a well-founded suspicion, not just any kind of suspicion. A well-founded suspicion means normally that there is already evidence available showing that this person is involved in some sort of illegal activity. It then becomes necessary to take certain peculiar steps and deploy peculiar technical means with the objective of proving that this person is indeed involved in some form of illegal activity, and then one must apply this operative processing at the proposal of the chief of security of the General Staff of the VJ and the decision is approved by the Chief of the General Staff of the VJ.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you say "unlawful activity" or "unauthorised activity," what sort of activity would you as the security administration be interested in or be looking into? We did speak about that yesterday, but could you just run it past us again, please.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, let me give you specific example. You have one or more persons secretly organising themselves in order to carry out a terrorist attack against a military facility or a member of the VJ, or, for example, a group of persons are secretly organising themselves in order to conduct espionage in order to obtain some secret documents such as state secrets concerning the use and deployment of the VJ, cases such as these.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General Gajic, do you know that security bodies or of the security administration at any point in time ever asked anyone from the VRS or the SVK to process any particular person in this way or to make a person the subject of their investigations?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Lukic. No such thing can be done without prior approval from the chief of security of the security administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Lines 18 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It appears that the witness has not answered the question of Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's fine. I will repeat that, the correction, though. Just to be perfectly specific, page 10, line 18, there is a blank there. I said the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, it's perfectly simple. Please answer my question, yes or no. Do you know if at any point in time anyone from the VJ asked anyone from the VRS or the SVK to subject a person to this sort of operative processing?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Lukic, no one ever did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you aware that anyone from the VRS or the SVK ever subjected a person to this kind of operative processing who belonged to the VJ? Did anyone ever approach you for approval of about anything like that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Lukic, not as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I'm not quite sure, because I don't understand B/C/S, and this is happening a second time. The questioning in English at page 11, line 9, says: "Were you aware that ..." Also, at page 10, line 16: "Do you know that ..." I don't know what the question was, but a reading of the sentence where you said, "Do you know that," the impression given to the reader is that you, the questioner, know that that happened, but you just want to know whether the witness knew if it did happen, and I don't want to suggest how the question should be asked, but -- I just want to understand that that's the question --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, yes, Your Honour. I understand your point. I understand fully. I fully understand what -- the question was interpreted properly, but it might give rise to some misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Both questions that I asked you, sir, the first question was this: Were you personally aware of any instance at any point in time where anyone at all from the VRS or the SVK subjected a person from the VJ to operative processing?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, no, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know if the VJ at any point required such --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could Mr. Lukic please repeat that question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please repeat your question, Mr. Lukic. The interpreters didn't hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sir, are you aware, General Gajic, whether anyone from the VJ at any point in time requested the security officers of the VRS or the SVK to conduct any operative processing like that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Lukic, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, does that make it more intelligible?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the President, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sir, you mentioned yesterday who the officers were of that body in the SVK, and you mentioned Rade Raseta. Did you at any time during the war actually see Mr. Raseta? Under what conditions, circumstances, and when?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At the time when I was transferred from the 1st army back to the security administration which was in early April 1994 and then all the way up until the end of the war, as far as I remember, I never saw Colonel Raseta.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you perhaps hear whether he came to the security administration in order to meet anyone there? What might have been the reasons? Do you have any information about that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I do know that Colonel Raseta came to the security administration. I can't tell you exactly how many times, whether twice, perhaps three times. He would normally see the chief of the security administration, and General Dimitrijevic was the person who introduced me to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General Dimitrijevic introduced you to him. But was he there because General Dimitrijevic invited him, or was there perhaps a different reason?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, the way the question is posed, it seems to call for speculation. The proper question, seems to me, was whether this witness knows why Mr. Raseta was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I asked a very specific question. Was he there because he was invited or not? I think that's probably the first thing that needs clarifying, and that's what I'm trying to do. Was it just an ad hoc thing, or was it actually at someone's request? And then my next question was going to be, does the witness know what the reason was? I don't think that is -- I mean, speculation in any shape or form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Objection overruled. However, I want to say to you if he answers "no" to your question as it stands, I don't know why you would have to ask him the reason, because then he wouldn't -- but anyway, carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very briefly, General Gajic, you knew that Raseta was there to see him. Did General Dimitrijevic ever tell you whether there was a reason for him coming, or an invitation or anything else?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: One question at a time, Mr. Lukic. One question at a time, not any reason or an invitation or anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did General Dimitrijevic tell you how Raseta came to be there?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Lukic, he never explained anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did General Dimitrijevic tell you whether he had requested any sort of report from Raseta? What were the facts they discussed, generally speaking?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, as for your first question, the answer is no. As for your second question, General Dimitrijevic informed me they talked about all the same subjects and in much the same way as previously with the security organs from the VRS, except this was now in relation to the Serbian Republic of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: OTP Exhibit P1926, please. [In English] This is P Exhibit 1926. [Interpretation] You mentioned Colonel Smiljanic as well, did you not, as being with the security of the SVK? I showed you this document during proofing. Can we please go straight to page 2 of this document. Could you please tell me what this is. What sort of a document is this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could we zoom into these documents, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Lukic, this is called information. It's a kind of document envisaged in an internal rule governing the work of the security organs. It's called "Instructions on documentation and records." So the purpose of a document like this is simply to inform.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Look at the date, the 1st of July, 1994. It was delivered to the security administration of the General Staff of the VJ and also to the security organ of the Main Staff of the SVK. Sir, do you remember seeing documents of this kind or indeed receiving documents of this kind during the war?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, as far as I remember, there may have been several documents like this from the SVK. As for the VRS, we received none at all or none that I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You've read this document. Let's not dwell on it, at least not in its entirety. If you believe it necessary, by all means go through the entire document, but tell me this: If you look at this document, do you find anything of potential relevance to you as a security officer of the VJ?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the document in its entirety relates to the situation in the autonomous province of Western Bosnia. The 5th Muslim Corps was deployed there and actually conducting combat operations. This is the border to the Republic of Serbian Krajina. This document discusses problems that occurred during the combat operations in which they engaged the 5th Muslim Corps. Some of the VRS forces were involved in that, and all of this happened in the autonomous province of Western Bosnia. This document addresses that issue specific and also says that as far as the leadership was concerned of the Autonomous Province of Western Bosnia, the leader at the time being Fikret Abdic, there were divisions within the leadership. Some favour the continuation of fighting against the 5th Muslim Corps. There were others who favoured a cessation to these hostilities and proposed that a part of the army [as interpreted] get directly involved in fighting the 5th Muslim Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is any of the information included in this document of any relevance to the security organs of the VJ?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, it was relevant since it potentially had a direct bearing on the Republic of Serbian Krajina, especially the Knin area. This was important terms of our assessments both in the level of the General Staff and also because we had other information indicating that Croatia was readying for offensive operations in co-operation with the Muslim forces in this very area.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On page 16, line 6, the witness said Serbian Army of Krajina and not just part of the army. All right. If we could now see another of the Prosecution's evidence or exhibits. This is P2334.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is a document of the General -- or, rather, Main Staff of the Serbian Army of Krajina, of the security department, of the 2nd of May, 1995, and it is sent to the security administration of the General Staff, signed by Colonel Raseta, who was in charge of the security. Did you see this document before, General?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember this report from the times when it was written, or do you only remember it from the time when I showed it to you? So can you remember whether you knew about this document earlier on?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, to be quite honest, I recall when you showed me this document, but I did recognise its contents.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just to make things clear, the contents of this document are related to the time of the Operation Flash, the attack against the Serbian Republic of Krajina. Could we please turn to page 3. The document is rather self-evident --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: While we're turning to page 3, Mr. Gajic, can you remember when you first saw this document ever?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I saw this document for the first time when it arrived to my administration, as far as I can recall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Here on page 3, which we can see now on the screen, we can see the stamp proving the reception. Is this the date when the document arrived to your administration, the 2nd of May?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So the very day it was written it was also logged in your administration. In this document there is mention of rocket attacks against Zagreb, the situation in Western Slavonia, and I am interested in what is written on page 3. Here we can see that discussions are mentioned among the leaders of the Republic of Srpska Krajina. Was this information in any way relevant for the security of the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, this information was not only relevant for the Army of Yugoslavia, as you said, and its security, in my mind it was very relevant for the leadership of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and their estimates and their decisions, because on this page 3 that you have now -- now shown me, the contents of what is written here have to do with the meeting of the Supreme Defence Council of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, and we can see that there was very clear division between the leaders. In one group we had the president, Milan Martic, and chief of Main Staff of the Army of Serbian Krajina, General Celeketic, and some others, and they were in favour of the continuation of the war. And there was another fraction which was in favour of negotiations and a peaceful solution. Why am I saying that this was very relevant not only for the army but also for the leadership of the state? Because at that time the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, our military and political leadership, were fully in favour of peace initiatives and the plan of the Contact Group as well as some other plans which aimed at resolving the problems between Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and Croatia in peaceful way. So this was something that actually was a kind of provocation for those efforts.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we please now look at another document, P2336. P2336. Now, this document was again signed by Colonel Raseta on the 26th of May, 1995, and it was sent to the commander of the Serbian Army of Krajina. I think it's self-evident, so I will not ask much about this report, but my question is, did you receive in the security administration the reports of this kind compiled by Colonel Raseta?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, no, because it is clearly stated here who was the addressee of this report, and it is specified very clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The next document I would like to show is yet another OTP exhibit, P1018. We will see yet another report by Colonel Raseta, dated 3rd of August, 1995, and addressed to the security administration of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, or specifically to General Dimitrijevic personally. You can see it on the screen, but I can see that you've found it in your folder as well. General, this document, did you see it before? If so, when? Do you remember this report?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, to be quite honest, when you showed me this document, then I recalled it. Obviously one can't remember all the details, but when I saw the contents, I recalled that report.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Given the date, which period does this report refer to? So which events does it refer to?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the date is August the 3rd, 1995. So this was two days before the Croatian Operation Storm against the Knin area.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If we could now move to page 4. So this is the last page both in the English and B/C/S. I apologise. We seem to need the previous page in English. What is written here under item 3? It says: "The situation on the territory." Without reading this out, I would like to know if what is written here was in any way relevant for the security of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, my answer is yes, and I can also tell you why. In the second paragraph of item 3, we can see that the president of the government of the Republic of Srpska Krajina, Milan Babic, invited ministers to flee from Knin, so to abandon the people and abandon the army, to leave them there. And in the previous paragraph we can see that among the population in the Republic of Serbian Krajina there was panic, possibly also caused by the Operation Flash which took place in May, and that the population was accusing the leadership of the Republic of Serbian Krajina for bringing about such a difficult situation. And obviously this was very significant, not only for the military leadership, but also for the political leadership. This information was needed for any decisions they might make, consider -- considering any peace plans.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After the Operation Storm, were there any consequences that were relevant for the security of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, there were numerous consequences. First of all, a large number of refugees, as far as I remember, more than 200.000 people came to the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and this was a large humanitarian but also security problem. Furthermore, a large number of members of the Serbian Army of Krajina and members of their families were in very dire situation. As regards our intelligence activities, we also felt more offensive, more specific activity coming from the direction of Croatia, because after that operation Tudjman was announcing another operation against Eastern Slavonia, which was the zone of responsibility of the 11th Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think this was a very good example now that you mentioned intelligence activities. Why did you describe this as intelligence activities rather than security activities when you mentioned Croatia?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was a foreign country and an enemy, and obviously it was the intelligence officers that were most involved, but also the counter-intelligence service could collect certain data, but this was not the bulk of their activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Both these reports by Colonel Raseta, one was related to the Operation Flash, that one of the 2nd of May, and the other one of the 3rd of August was related to the imminent Operation Storm, did you know given the exceptional circumstances at the time whether your security administration requested any reports from Colonel Raseta, or were these reports sent at his own initiative? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, as far as I know, we did not request any such reports, but it was the estimate of Colonel Raseta to send them, and I can only applaud his estimates.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we please have a look at yet another OTP's exhibit. This was P1084. With this we will move to some issues related to another army. I don't believe that this is a correct document, so -- P1084. I apologise. This may have been my mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I gave you a wrong number, and also we need to move into closed session for the next document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. And what is the document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This may have been marked wrongly, General, in your binder. This is a document of the security administration sent to the sector for security issues of the Main Staff of the VRS, signed by Captain Beara -- or, rather, it was the document coming from the Main Staff's security department and sent to the security administration of the General Staff. Do you remember this document from previous times?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you say you remember it, do you remember it from those days?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On the second page we can see the stamp proving the reception of the document. I don't believe that the date is legible, but do you remember that you saw this document at approximately the time when it was written in 1995?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, what do you know concerning the contents of this document?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I remember this document because it was created in some very specific circumstances. It is dated 11th of August, 1995. And on the 5th of August the Croatian Army's Operation Storm was launched against the Knin area of Krajina. What preceded it was the Operation Flash in May of 1995. These two operations resulted in a huge number of refugees, several hundreds of thousands of refugees. And in this document we can read about a very specific situation. Actually, it is telling us that we can expect a large number of refugees also from the territory of Republika Srpska -- or, actually, from the territory of the municipality of Drvar. And this operation was led by the legitimate War Presidency which invited the population to abandon the territory of the municipality of Drvar and some other municipalities which would obviously cause yet another security problem and humanitarian problem for the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and it could also have very negative consequences for the Army of Republika Srpska. Obviously, once the population leaves the territory, it is well known that the army will follow, and this is why I can remember the contents of this document. I believe this was a very significant document both for the army and for the political leadership of our country.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: From the time you first came to work with the security administration in 1994 and all the way up until the end of 1995, do you remember how many reports like this from Mr. Beara did you receive in this shape or format?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, we did not receive any of these in writing. I can't remember if there was perhaps the occasional report or not. But during those contacts and the visits by Beara, one of his subordinates, we would hear oral reports like this, stories like this one, corroborating what this document says.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did the security administration have any information about any information leaks from the VJ, information being leaked to any other army?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we please have Defence 65 ter document 00886D. [In English] 00886D.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you still want to stay in private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is a document by the corps commander of the special units of the VJ, Colonel Miodrag Panic. The date is September 1995. Can you tell us what this document talks about, General?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, this document was produced pursuant to an order from the Chief of the General Staff, dated the 25th of August, 1995. This is in relation to some leaks of classified military information concerning equipment, both equipment used for combat and noncombat equipment, available to the VJ. This was leaked to unauthorised officials from the Republic of Serbian Krajina and the RS. The actual information was leaked by sources within the VJ. This is a warning by the Chief of the General Staff, and then the corps commander of the special units conveyed this to his subordinates. This is a warning and a ban, meaning this would no longer be tolerated.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The first paragraph is quite specific about the fact that information leaks such as this were quite typical in terms of the equipment in the possession of the VJ and its material war reserves. Why was it important to keep this kind of information from the VRS or the SVK?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, there are two reasons why this would have been important. The first reason being this information might eventually have reached foreign intelligence agencies, and then these agencies would have known whatever they needed to know about the combat capability of the VJ and its equipment and material resources. Secondly, to be quite honest, there were constant complaints from the SVK and the VRS to the tune of, You have the equipment, you have the means, and yet you're not giving us a hand. Therefore, rumours were being spread that were simply untrue and quite biased, despite which all these roomers had certain consequences that we had to deal with.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May this document be received, Your Honours, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D267. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, did the security administration have any contacts with any representatives of foreign armies in the FRY? What sort of contacts? Do you have any personal knowledge of anything like that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, a security administration had contacts with a number of military diplomatic representatives of foreign countries accredited in Belgrade. Most of those representatives were from countries of the West, Western countries. Normally they would request these meetings or contacts. There were also briefings organised by our administration for liaising with foreign representatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me specifically, if you remember, who was there, who you met. Did you personally meet anyone?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I personally did not meet anyone, not up until 1997, which was when we had some contacts with people from the American agencies. Normally it was the chief of the security administration, General Dimitrijevic, who did have contacts.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did he pass information along to you, who he met and what they talked about? I want know about up until the end of the war, the end of 1995.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I was up to date on everything. General Dimitrijevic would tell me who he was on his way to meet. Sometimes he wanted documents prepared for him which he could then discuss with these men, the representatives, and every time he was back from those meetings -- or before he -- he would ever about, he would invariably inform the Chief of the General Staff, he would confer with him, and often he went to see the Chief of the General Staff to discuss this with him and pick topics potentially to be discussed with these representatives. Every time he came back, General Dimitrijevic would go to the Chief of the General Staff to convey to him whatever was discussed at those meetings. In a very general way I, too, was informed about the subject matter discussed at those meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think there's an error on page 26, line 20. He said sometimes he wanted information, and the reference here is to document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, just to make sure. I'm not sure I understood myself. Did General Dimitrijevic ask for documents to be prepared for him or just for information to be provided for those meetings?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Information, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was the substance of those talks? Did General Dimitrijevic tell you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the gist of all the talks was this: The military and diplomatic representatives, particularly of the most influential Western countries, wanted to know about the views and positions of the military and even State leadership vis-a-vis the peace initiatives of the international community. Secondly, most of those representatives were fair. They would provide their own assessments and views that were sometimes helpful to us at the security administration, but also to the state leaders in their work with these peace initiatives, agreeing to the Contact Group plan and all the other initiatives that were in progress back then.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did General Dimitrijevic ever tell you whether any crimes were discussed at any of those meetings, committed by whoever?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Dimitrijevic never mentioned that as one of the subjects being discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember any names, what those people were called, the high representatives that General Dimitrijevic met?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, Mr. Lukic. The USA representative Hutchouse [as interpreted], who was followed by Colonel Fischer. Colonel Ariolf [as interpreted] on behalf of Italy, he was a military envoy. It has been a long time. That's as much as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Our next document -- yesterday, at the beginning we spoke about the information that you had about groups secretly arming themselves before the clashes broke out. Did the security administration ever get any information concerning citizens of other countries who were members of the BH Army, Croatia's army, or any other army?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Mr. Lukic. That was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we please have Defence 65 ter 00719D. This is a document by the chef de cabinet of the General Staff of the VJ. Dispatch on the 11th of February, 1992, to the Federal Ministry of Foreign Affairs. Can we please go to page 2 of the document. General, what is this? I believe the document speaks for itself. What sort of information is at stake here?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, if you look at the heading, you see what the document is about and what the information is about. It's about the role of Croatia. As is well known at the time Croatia was already an internationally recognised country. So this discusses the role of Croatia in the illegal arming and making it possible for foreign mercenaries to cross its territory and use their civilian and military infrastructure in order to reach Bosnia and Herzegovina by illegal channels even before the clashes ever broke out in 1992 over in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and even before Bosnia and Herzegovina became an independent country. Its independence was proclaimed on the 7th of April, 1992. The international recognition followed. So Croatia was counteracting the resolutions of the Security Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Why would the security administration be interested in any --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could Mr. Lukic please be asked to repeat the question. We didn't understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Gajic. Mr. Lukic, the interpreter didn't hear the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Why did the security administration want to know about such information as mentioned in the document?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, we wanted to know about this type of information because for the most part we are dealing here with members of the Mujahedin, who posed a certain security threat to the security of the FRY. Even back then, we were facing the problem of Kosovo. We already had information at the time indicating that some of these mercenaries, particularly the Mujahedin, were seeping into Kosovo across the Albanian border, even as early on as 1993. Therefore, it was particularly important for us to be familiar with this type of information. And if I may just add something. It was particularly important because as early on as this, we were receiving information showing that in Zenica a camp had been set up for the training of these Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would that be an appropriate --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we might just have a this document received, please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D268.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. We will then be at an appropriate time. We'll take a break and come back at 4.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, I will move to an entirely different subject. We will talk about the events of February 1995 [as interpreted], the events in Srebrenica and Zepa. Could we please see on the screen document from the 65 ter list, 00663D. [In English] 00663D. [Interpretation] Can you see it on the screen? If not, you also have it in your binder. This is an information on the state of the Muslim forces in the Zepa enclave, dated 14th of July, 1995, sent by the 2nd administration of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia. Did you find this document?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: First of all, can you tell us something about the form of this document. Whose document was it, and who was it sent to?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, this is an information of the 2nd administration of the General Staff of the VJ that was sent daily, first of all to the operations centre, to the Chief of the General Staff, and then to the security administration, although I need to say that not all the documents of this kind, informations, reached the security administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Down there we can see that this information was to be submitted to the Colonel-General Momcilo Perisic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the first paragraph we can see -- I will read it out because it is a short paragraph. "Having taken the Srebrenica enclave, units of the VRS concentrated their forces around the Zepa enclave, and on the 12th of July, 1995, they issued an ultimatum to the commander of the 1st Zepa Brigade ..." I am particularly interested in what is written in paragraph 4, where it says that one 80-man strong Muslim unit encircled a Ukrainian company at 1235 hours and did not allow it to move. Were you aware, General, in those days of problems in Zepa, particularly in relation to the Ukrainian battalion?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was the source of your information?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, it was first of all General Dimitrijevic who presented this problem to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was it that General Dimitrijevic said?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Dimitrijevic told me during our morning meetings that I described yesterday that General Perisic will have to go, if I remember well, he said, To Mladic, to Republika Srpska. So I asked him why, what was the problem? And he told me, Well, it seems that there was a serious problem regarding the Ukrainian battalion. And he added that it seemed that the Ukrainian battalion was encircled. And bearing in mind everything that was happening with the peace talks, this could become a serious problem that could have some unwanted consequences since these were international forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm not objecting to the admission of the document. However, I do have some concerns about the quality of the translation, and for that reason I would suggest perhaps this should be MFI'd at this time. For example, there appears to be some text in the B/C/S original at the bottom which we don't find -- at least I don't find in the English. And at the same time, at the centre of the page, towards the bottom of the English translation, we see, "This is a true copy of the original," certified by a signature and stamped, but I don't see any such markings in the original. So I'm wondering perhaps if this could be sent to CLSS for a revised translation. If it could be MFI'd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no objections, Your Honour. I agree. We did get this officially from CLSS. It's an official translation. Nevertheless, if there's a need to run a check, we might as well MFI the document for our present purposes. What Mr. Saxon just said is perfectly right. It needs checking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Just two questions from me before we admit it. When you introduced this topic now, you said -- and this is at page 30, line 18: "General, I'll move to an entirely different subject." I see it says difficult subject. You said different subject. "I will move to February 1995." Now, this is the only document that you have shown the witness since that introduction, and I see it's July 1995. Now, I wanted to be sure with you, did you mean -- did you say February 1995? Or did you say something else, because --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Because February 1995, the events in Srebrenica and Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have done very well to observe that, Your Honour. It must be my error or the interpreter's error. I was trying to say that I was moving on to an entirely different subject, and secondly, I mentioned July 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The second question is, I -- looking at this document, I'm not able -- looking at the English part of translation, I'm not able to determine whom it comes from.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd best just ask the witness perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Witness, can we see who --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And who it is going to.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [previous translation continues] ... and who it is addressed to.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, based on what the document says, who is it sending this document and who is the addressee?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Lukic, the bottom of this document states 2nd administration of the General Staff of the VJ on the right-hand side. On the left-hand side just below the date, the 14th of July, 1995, delivered to Colonel-General Momcilo Perisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you for that, but who does it come from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the 2nd administration, the military intelligence administration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Of which army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The VJ, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Where do we see -- where do we see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Okay. The Judge has shown me. Thank you so much. Okay. The document is admitted into evidence. And may it please be given an exhibit number and be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit 269, marked for identification. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now I would like to see another document on the screen. This is from the 65 ter list, 00666D. This is the information number 115 of the 2nd administration of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, dated the 18th of July, 1995. And it is mentioned here that the liaison officer of "the Ukrainian battalion in Glina approached us with a request following the capturing of a Ukrainian UNPROFOR company in Gorazde to receive three representatives of their General Staff in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and help them get in touch with the General Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska in order to extract or liberate the above-mentioned company." General, do you know whether General Perisic went there in those days as it was announced to you by General Dimitrijevic? So did he go to the Main Staff of the VRS and why?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know about that because General Dimitrijevic told me that General Perisic went to Republika Srpska to try and help resolve this situation. First of all, to see for himself what this problem was all about and then to try and help for this company to be de-blocked or released.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether the Ukrainian battalion left the territory of Zepa in those days? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I can't remember that, but I do remember that I read later on in an information or another document, I can't recall precisely, that that battalion was de-blocked and that they once again regained some normal conditions within which they could operate.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D270. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did the security administration receive any information concerning any events on the River Drina following the events in Zepa, so anything to -- to the content that somebody swam over Drina, possibly trying to flee?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was it that you can remember concerning this?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 31st of July, we received a telegram from the 2nd Military District, and this was actually from the security organ of the 15th Border Battalion, which reported their direct superiors, and this was the security organ of the Uzice Corps, and as I said, we received this from the security organ of the 2nd Army, and the Uzice Corps at the time belonged to the 2nd Army. So we received the information that a certain number of members of the Muslim army swam over the Drina River and thus came to the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know for how long a period of time this lasted and how many people swam across the river?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, it lasted for several days, possibly 3rd and 4th of August. And if I remember well, it was several hundreds of members of the Muslim armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What happened to those people thereafter? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, in the first information, we learned that the command immediately set up a three-member reception commission. If I recall well, the names of the members of this commission were also included in the information received. So they were registering all these people. Quite a few of them were in poor condition. They caught colds or they were wet, so their reception was organised. So the security organ was also engaged to make sure that nothing would happen to those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you say the command, which command are you talking about? Who organised this?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, this was the command of the 15th Border Battalion. And through the chain of command, they informed their superiors at the Uzice Corps about this issue, and further on through the 2nd Army, the Chief of the General Staff and the General Staff as such also received this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It is perfectly clear to me, but for the record, we just have to make sure we know which army we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. Lukic. The Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could we please see on the screen document from the 65 ter list 01131D.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, you can see how this was translated by our translation service, and I need to inform you that we are talking about a -- a set of 12 documents, each document consisting of four or five pages of names, and the translation service thus far provided this kind of translation, and if you allow me, I will now use this document with the witness, and we will focus only on the names that are legible. If Your Honours would like us to provide the entire document, then I will request the translation service to do that, but I know that this is their usual way of doing it when it is difficult to read the names. So I would just like to go through some of the items with the witness and I will see what the reaction will be of Your Honours and my learned colleague from the Prosecution. So all I can tell you now is that we are talking about 12 documents, each of them containing four or five pages, and this is the kind of information contained in these documents. But if you allow me, would I like first of all to ask the witness certain questions and possibly he will clarify the meaning of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What is it, sir, that we can see in front of us now?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, this is a list of members of the Muslim armed forces who, after the 31st of July, 1995, and thereafter, came to the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and it also contains some data.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us which data were entered into this document.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, first of all maybe I can comment on the heading. You can see "Military post number 2493," and you can see the date. This is the 1st of August. Yes, the 1st of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a second, sir. You said 1998.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, 1995. So this is the military post designating the 15th Border Battalion. And here we can see a list that contains different columns. First of all, the number, then the name, father's name, and the last name. In the third column we can see the date of birth and the place of birth. So the third column is divided into two. Then the fourth column is unit that the person comes from, and the last column is their occupation. And at the end of each list you can see that the person who compiled the list signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just to clarify the numbers. So column 5 is the membership of the unit, and column 6 the occupation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could we please see the last page of this document in the B/C/S, and this is the portion that has been translated for Their Honours in English. Here we can see the hand-over commission and the reception or admittance commission. Here where we can see the hand-over commission, the persons listed here, which institution they came from?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, we can see that these were officers of the 15th Border Battalion of the Army of Yugoslavia. I can read their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That will not be necessary. Can you tell us this reception commission or admittance commission, which institution they came from?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, these were representatives of the Ministry of the Interior, and you can see that the commission consisted of three members who acted as a commission, as a group, when they received these persons, and this is why they signed this here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In this column which says "Unit," we can see certain data. Could you tell us members of whose army were those based on the data entered under "Unit"?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, we can see that these were members of the Muslim armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And the last number on this list is 53. So it says, "Concluded with number 53;" is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have another list that was typewritten which is probably legible a bit more, but now I would like to tender this list, this document, into evidence. I suggest that we do not go document by document, but because they're of the same type, if my learned colleague from the OTP has into objection, then I would not put all of these documents before the witness, but I suggest that we tender them as such.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I don't have an objection to proceeding that way. However, I do have a question regarding translation and what exactly then is being admitted. Is it Mr. Lukic's proposition to tender each of these lists in their entirety, because if that's the case, then I would ask that we get a full English translation and that it be marked for identification at this time until we get the full translations. If he's only using excerpts as an example, then would I simply like that to be entered into record that that is what's -- that is the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Given the data entered into these lists, that these were members of identified units, I would suggest that we translate these entire lists and that we then tender them as such or that we, rather, receive them as such, and in meantime we can MFI them. Your Honour, if you allow me, maybe I could show you another example in the meantime which is typewritten, so possibly it would be better even for people who do not understand Serbian, because you could see what kind of data are entered into those lists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't think there's any problem with the kind of data that's entered into the list. The problem is the one that was raised by Mr. Saxon, and you seem to agree to his suggestion, that we mark them for identification and we get them translated, and then we can move on to the next point. Okay? Then the documents are admitted into evidence. May they please be given an exhibit number and be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D271, marked for identification. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just so that we are clear, are the parties agreed, in fact, that the entire 12 documents that you referred to are being so admitted and they will be so translated? Or is it just this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I suggested -- now my case manager informed me that there are 14 lists. Could you hold on just a second, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. And they under 14 different numbers on our 65 ter list. So I would propose for all of them to now be given their MFI numbers without presenting them one by one to the witness, or possibly we can also do it outside the courtroom, whatever the secretariat believes best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I guess you have no objection to that, Mr. Saxon?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Then we'll do it so, and can it be done outside court, and then you can move on to the next point. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. While we are still on this subject, could the witness please be shown 65 ter 00851D. The document has been translated into English in its entirety, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic, what does this document tell us? Whose document is it? And can you see it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. This is a document by the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serbia, specifically the Uzice Secretariat of the Interior. The date is the 3rd of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Does this document talk about the same developments that you described a while ago?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, Mr. Lukic. This is a list of ethnic Muslims who belonged to the Muslim armed forces, and that is what we have been talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May this be received, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit 272. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could we please have 65 ter 00821D. The date is the 8th of March, 1996. Wait a minute, sir. We want this on our screens. As soon as you can see it, tell us whose document it is and what it's about. Who is the author of this document, General?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is information on the living conditions among the members of the Muslim armed forces in the reception centres of Mitrovo Polje and Vranicka [as interpreted] Polje. The document was produced, as you said, on the 8th of March, 1996, by the SUP of Uzice, which was under the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There is a reference here to a total of 799 persons in paragraph 1, the time period being from the 31st of July to the 25th of October. General, based on this report are these the same persons that you mentioned a minute ago?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Moreover, the document states that the public was informed about the active involvement of the MUP, UNHCR, and the International Red Cross, members of foreign diplomatic representations came as well, the embassies, and international media as well. I'm just summing up? I'm trying to avoid reading the entire document. I did show you this during proofing. Did you know at the time about what this says. And is this really what happened?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I knew that at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Page 2, there is something that I find interesting. If you could please comment, sir. It's the last paragraph on that page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next page in the English, please. Your Honours, it's the sentence at the top of the page. Foreign currency is mentioned there and an exchange office that was established.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether any money was seized from those people? Were there any problems like that at all?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Lukic, there were no problems like that at all. As you suggest, International Red Cross was informed immediately as well as the UNHCR, and they made a great effort to put these people up.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What became of these persons later on, if you know, sir.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I know that those persons were allowed to decide for themselves as to what their next destination would be upon leaving the reception centres. As far as I know, most of them headed west, most of them through Hungary. Every security measure available was taken in the process.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May this be received, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D273. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Another document on this same topic, 65 ter 00822D. Sir, are you familiar with this document? What can you tell us about it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed I am, Mr. Lukic. The date is the 26th of October, 1995. It talks about a report produced by two forensic epidemiological teams or health teams who examined all the members of the Muslim armed forces in these two reception centres here. They performed medical checks and duly submitted a report about that. They also actually signed this report after they proposed certain measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There are references here to two facilities. One of them is the Vranisko [as interpreted] Polje reception centre; and the other is the Mitrovo Polje reception centre. Do you in fact know that the Muslims who had swum across the Drina River in early August were in those reception centres?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic, I actually knew that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May this be received, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D274. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
